h1: Burnt rubber and drain notes from mercaptans in packaged beer
title: Mercaptan Notes in Packaged Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: Where burnt rubber, drain and rotten cabbage notes in packaged beer come from, from yeast autolysis and light strike to spoilage bacteria.
teaser: A beer that smells of a blocked drain after a month in the can has a sulphur problem. Finding out which one is the job.
standfirst: Mercaptans, also called thiols, are sulphur compounds with some of the strongest smells in brewing. In packaged beer they point to a handful of causes: dying yeast, light, warm storage or anaerobic spoilage bacteria. Each needs a different fix.
sections:
Mercaptans give beer a family of unpleasant sulphur smells: blocked drain, rotten cabbage, sewer, burnt rubber and, in the case of light strike, skunk. They are distinct from the rotten egg of hydrogen sulphide, though they often appear together. Thresholds are extremely low. Methanethiol, the simplest mercaptan, is noticeable at a few micrograms per litre, so a small amount of breakdown is enough to spoil a beer.

The important clue is timing. A beer that left the brewery clean and developed these notes weeks later in the can or bottle has a problem in the package, not in the brewhouse.

When yeast cells die and break down, they release their contents into the beer, including sulphur amino acids that turn into mercaptans. In packaged beer this happens most in bottle-conditioned and unfiltered products that carry live yeast and then sit warm. A bottle-conditioned ale stored at 30 °C for two months is a good candidate. Autolysis also brings meaty, brothy notes, covered in our guide to yeast autolysis.

The fix is about yeast counts and temperature: condition with a modest, healthy pitch, keep the yeast count in the package no higher than needed and keep packaged beer cold.

Light strike is a specific mercaptan, 3-methyl-2-butene-1-thiol, formed when ultraviolet and visible light break down hop iso-alpha acids in the presence of riboflavin. It smells of skunk. Many drinkers describe it as burnt rubber instead. Clear and green glass offer little protection. Brown glass blocks much more of the damaging light and cans block all of it.

A beer that is fine in the can and skunky in clear glass from the same batch is light struck, not infected. Our guide to light-struck beer and bottle colour covers this in detail.

The most serious cause is infection by strictly anaerobic bacteria, chiefly Pectinatus and Megasphaera. They grow in low oxygen, unpasteurised packaged beer, especially lower alcohol beers with a relatively high pH. They produce hydrogen sulphide, methanethiol and fatty acids such as propionic and butyric acid, giving a revolting combination of drain, rotten egg and vomit. Affected packages often turn hazy too.

Ironically, good low oxygen packaging makes these bacteria more likely to thrive if they get in. They tend to live in the filler, in conveyors and in hard to clean spots of the packaging line. A cluster of affected bottles from one filling head points straight at the source.
How to work out which cause you have

A short decision path helps:

  • Skunky, only in clear or green glass, fine in cans or brown bottles: light strike.
  • Meaty, brothy, worse in warm-stored bottle-conditioned beer, no haze change: autolysis.
  • Drain and vomit, haze, gushing or sediment, worse with time, random or clustered packages: suspect bacteria and send samples for anaerobic plating.

For bacteria, ordinary aerobic plates will show nothing. The lab needs anaerobic media and incubation. Pasteurisation, typically in the range of 15 to 25 pasteurisation units for beer, controls these organisms, as does sterile filtration. Unpasteurised craft beer relies entirely on line hygiene and cold storage.
Why Indian distribution raises the stakes

Every one of these causes speeds up with heat. Autolysis, bacterial growth and the general chemistry of staling all run faster at 30 °C than at 4 °C. Packaged craft beer in India often moves through warehouses and trucks without refrigeration, then sits in a shop fridge that is switched off overnight. A beer that tastes clean at the brewery gate can arrive at a bar weeks later with a sulphur problem that nobody at the brewery ever tasted.

That is why market samples matter. Buying your own beer back from shops in different cities and tasting it against a cold-stored reference from the same batch, shows what the distribution chain is doing to it. It is cheap, it is humbling and it often explains complaints that a brewery's own tasting room never sees.
Rubber taint from new hoses and seals

One more source sits outside chemistry textbooks: new rubber hoses, gaskets and seals that are not food grade or were not properly conditioned before use. They can give beer a genuine rubber or chemical smell. It usually shows right after maintenance, fades as the parts age and affects every package from that run equally. Ask what changed on the line that week.

Your first step: keep a few cans and bottles from every batch, store half cold and half at room temperature and taste them at four and eight weeks. Mercaptan problems almost always show up in the warm set first.
faqs: What causes drain or rotten cabbage smells in packaged beer?
Mercaptans from yeast autolysis, light strike or anaerobic spoilage bacteria such as Pectinatus and Megasphaera.
How can I tell light strike from infection?
Light strike shows in clear or green glass and not in cans from the same batch. Infection tends to bring haze, gushing and drain or vomit notes that worsen over time.
Why does warm storage make it worse?
Heat speeds yeast autolysis and bacterial growth, both of which release mercaptans.
Yes. New hoses, gaskets or seals that are not food grade or not conditioned can give a rubber note, usually right after maintenance.
